newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech NATO, EU bid seen aided by Kohl, de Charette.
newsitem.headline: Czech NATO, EU bid seen aided by Kohl, de Charette.

text.p: Czech plans to join NATO and the European Union may be boosted by high-profile visits to Prague by German and French leaders in coming days but analysts cautioned on Thursday that the road ahead may not be so simple.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl is due in Prague next Tuesday and Wednesday to sign a joint declaration meant to tie up the bilateral loose ends of World War Two and including explicit support for Czech membership of Western organisations.
Before that, on Friday, French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette is in town and French officials say he is carrying a message of support for Czech membership by as early as 2000.

"It will demonstrate that the two countries which are the engines of European integration are really interested in what is going on here," said Jiri Pehe, head of research at the Open Media Research Institute.

Czech officials hope the signing of the agreement by Kohl and Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus will give fresh impetus to Prague's bids for membership of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) and the EU.

"When you have the Germans actually write something down, it is an important obligation for them. Their support for the Czechs is an important matter," a senior Czech diplomat told reporters on Wednesday.
The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are the leading contenders to be the next new members of NATO and the EU. But analysts warned against reading too much into German backing.

"It is important that it is specifically put in the declaration but if the Czech government got into problems (in negotiations), it is difficult to imagine what Germany could do," said Bela Plechanovova, lecturer in international relations at Prague's Charles University.

In the Czech-German accord, drawn up after two years of delicate talks, Bonn expresses its sorrow for the 1938-45 Nazi occupation of the Czech lands and Prague its regret for Czech brutality in the post-war expulsion of ethnic Sudeten Germans.
The deal has been criticised by families and supporters of Sudeten Germans -- mostly living now in the southern state of Bavaria -- and by Czech communists and ultra-right Republicans.

"No one knows what this declaration will do in reality in either country. It may have the healing effect everybody is talking about, it may radicalise Sudeten Germans and the leftists is this country and worsen the situation," said Pehe.
The accord must still be ratified by both parliaments.
Germany is the main political sponsor of East European states in their integration bids and the Czech Republic is the last not to have signed a reconciliation agreement with Bonn.
Plechanovova said the centre-right coalition government had stressed the accord's importance to Czech integration hopes but had not begun serious debate on what membership would mean.
An opinion poll published earlier this week by the Factum agency showed 55 percent of respondents supported EU membership while only 37 percent agreed with joining NATO.
"That could be a danger because if you look at Austria and Sweden before the (EU membership) discussions, support was higher," said Pehe.
Many Czechs are wary of joining another military alliance after spending more than 40 years under Soviet domination.
De Charette flies to Prague from Budapest, where he is accompanying President Jacques Chirac on a visit. The French president is due to visit the Czech Republic later this year.
